summary: A 1976 note on the syntax used to specify addresses in network mail. It looks at how addresses can be written so that mail systems on different hosts can understand them.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 720 proposes a more structured way to write network mail addresses. It separates a person's name from the mailbox address and adds forms for mailing lists and secondary mailboxes.

questions: how were mailing lists handled in 1976
how did rfc 720 format mail addresses
how did the proposal represent mailing lists
what is a secondary file in rfc 720
subtitle: A proposed syntax that separates personal names, user IDs, mailboxes, and hosts.

tldr.problem: The existing network-mail syntax did not conveniently separate a person's name from the address and made long lists and secondary mailboxes difficult to express.
tldr.mechanism: The proposal defines address components for a person, user ID, optional secondary file, and host, and permits named lists to be expanded or referenced by pathname.
tldr.outcome: RFC 720 proposes additions and replacements to the address syntax in RFC 680 and provides a modified BNF grammar.

today: RFC 720 is a proposal to augment the network-mail syntax described in RFC 680. Its stated intent is to serve until a more complete mail syntax and protocol are specified.

sections.title: Addressing Problems
sections.content:
The RFC identifies several difficulties with existing mail addresses: a person's name is not the same as an address, mailing lists may be long, a message may need to carry its recipient list for replies, and a user may want mail delivered to a secondary mailbox or file.

The current syntax does not conveniently separate a human name from the address. The memo proposes a syntax for address fields supplied by the user.
sections.plainLanguage: A mail address can identify a computer mailbox without clearly naming the person. Long lists and extra mailboxes also need ways to be represented.

sections.title: Address Components and Mailing Lists
sections.content:
The proposed address can include a person's name, a user ID, an optional secondary file, and a host. A group can have a name followed by its members, or a pathname can identify the file containing the group list.

The proposal permits matching bracket pairs such as parentheses, square brackets, braces, and angle brackets. Quotation marks are used for names containing characters that could confuse the syntax.
sections.plainLanguage: The format keeps a person's name separate from the user ID and host. A mailing list can include its members or point to a file containing them.

sections.title: Formal Grammar and Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives examples of ordinary addresses, named lists carried with a message, lists represented by a pathname, and names written separately from addresses. It then provides modified BNF definitions for address fields, individual addresses, groups, and optional secondary files.

The document says this syntax is for communication between systems and does not necessarily describe what a user types in a mail program.
sections.plainLanguage: Examples show how the proposed parts fit together, and a grammar defines how a system can parse them. The wire syntax need not match the user interface.
